en.body:
The digital landscape of streaming is constantly evolving, and this week brings a fascinating mix of genres and directorial voices to your screens. For fans of internet-bred horror and uncanny aesthetics, **Backrooms** is a must-watch. Directed by **Kane Parsons**, this film plunges viewers into the disorienting, liminal spaces that have captivated online communities. The opening minutes serve as a perfect primer, showcasing a found-footage recording of a researcher lost in an endless, unnerving environment. The production design, with its mirrored signs and melted furniture, creates an immediately unsettling atmosphere, amplified by the unseen forces that stalk our protagonist. As the echoes of footsteps grow louder and the tape ends in devastation, we're introduced to Clark, a failed architect whose story unfolds in this chilling narrative.

Also premiering on streaming platforms this week is **Brand New Landscape**, a debut feature from director **Yuiga Danzuka**. This film, a festival favorite that premiered at Cannes Directors' Fortnight, explores themes of family and confronting the past. It centers on siblings Ren and Emi, who have been estranged from their father for a decade. The narrative grapples with the choice of whether to drive away from difficult memories or turn back to face them. The performances, particularly from **Kurosawa Kodai** in his first lead role, are expected to be a significant draw for those who appreciate character-driven dramas with a strong emotional core.

## Diving into the Digital Unknown

The arrival of **Backrooms** on streaming is a significant moment for creators who have built their careers on platforms like YouTube. **Kane Parsons**, a 20-year-old YouTuber, has translated the viral internet phenomenon into a cinematic experience. The film's strength lies in its ability to evoke dread through its uncanny production design and low-resolution, period-appropriate visuals. The disquieting nature of the liminal space, combined with the escalating tension of being pursued by an unseen entity, taps into primal fears. This is a film that understands the power of suggestion and atmosphere, making it a compelling watch for anyone fascinated by the uncanny valley and the aesthetics of digital decay.

## Facing the Echoes of the Past

**Brand New Landscape** offers a more introspective journey, focusing on the complexities of familial relationships and the weight of unspoken history. The film's premise, centered on estranged siblings confronting their past, promises a narrative rich with emotional resonance. Its festival success indicates a strong critical reception and a compelling story that connects with audiences on a personal level. For viewers who enjoy films that explore the nuances of human connection and the challenges of reconciliation, **Brand New Landscape** is an excellent addition to the streaming library. The source material hints at a thoughtful exploration of choices and consequences, making it a standout in this week's new releases.

## What's Next

These new arrivals join a growing slate of diverse films available to stream. Keep an eye on platforms like HBO Max and Fandor for these and other curated selections that highlight both established filmmakers and exciting new voices in cinema.

content_raw: Each week we highlight the noteworthy titles that have recently hit streaming platforms in the United States. Check out this week’s selections below and past round-ups  here . Backrooms (Kane Parsons) The opening five minutes serve as an ideal primer for anybody unfamiliar with Parsons’  Backrooms  web series, and who maybe need a little extra convincing that a 20-year-old YouTuber has some juice: a found-footage recording of a researcher lost in the endless liminal space who gets chased by some unseen force of evil. Even when seen in the extremely low resolution of period-appropriate early-1990s camcorders, there’s something immediately disquieting about the uncanny production design (courtesy of Perkins’ regular collaborator Danny Vermette), where signs appear as their mirror image, various objects of furniture have melted into the floor, and the only living souls are seagulls. It’s an uncomfortable space to be in before the echoes of footsteps begin gathering speed behind our cameraman, and as this tape ends in offscreen devastation, we flash forward approximately ten days to meet Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a failed architect and owner of the fabulously named furniture store Cap’n Clark’s Ottoman Empire. – Alistair R. ( full review ) Where to Stream: HBO Max Brand New Landscape (Yuiga Danzuka) A favorite on the festival circuit last year, where it premiered at Cannes Directors’ Fortnight, Yuiga Danzuka’s debut feature is on Fandor. Blake Simons said in their review , “When confronted with the past, do you drive away or turn back to face it? Siblings Ren (Kurosaki Kodai, in his first lead role) and Emi (Mai Kiryu) have been estranged from their father (Ken’ichi Endô) for the ten years since he chose a new work opportunity in Tokyo. Ren, now a florist, notices a familiar name on the neighboring workstation’s order card. Propelled by emotion, not logic, he takes on the delivery himself, arriving to discover his father staring back at him through the floor-to-ceiling window of a major exhibition. Clutching the arrangement tight to his chest, there’s a heavy burden to carry.” Where to Stream: Fandor Dead Souls (Alex Cox) Repo Man , Sid and Nancy , and Walker director Alex Cox makes his return with a Western adaptation of Nikolai Gogol’s classic novel  Dead Souls . In his interview with the director , Jackson Diianni said, “Having read  Dead Souls , it’s not surprising that it would appeal to Cox. For one thing, there’s a very self-referential quality to the writing. The narrator often speaks directly to the reader about the novel itself, calling to mind some of Cox’s well-known postmodern touches: the generic food labels of  Repo Man  (1984), the intentional anachronisms of  Walker  (1987), Malcolm McLaren’s finger guns and Sid Vicious’ fantasy of shooting the audience in  Sid and Nancy  (1986).
